content: Childhood vaccination is one of the most effective methods for parents to protect infants, children, and teenagers from 16 potentially serious diseases. These vaccine-preventable diseases can be severe, may require hospitalization, and in some cases, can even be fatal, particularly in infants and young children. Vaccines work by helping the immune system develop immunity through the simulation of an infection. This simulated infection does not cause illness but prompts the immune system to produce T-lymphocytes and antibodies. Occasionally, after receiving a vaccine, the body’s response to this simulated infection may result in minor symptoms, such as a fever. These mild symptoms are normal and indicate that the body is building immunity. Once the simulated infection resolves, the immune system retains a supply of memory T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes. These cells are capable of recognizing and combating the disease in the future. However, it typically takes a few weeks for the body to generate these T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes after vaccination. Consequently, if an individual is exposed to a disease shortly before or after vaccination, they may still develop symptoms and contract the disease because the vaccine has not yet had sufficient time to provide protection. The childhood vaccination schedule outlines the recommended immunizations for children and adolescents up to 18 years of age, as per the CDC's 2017 guidelines. For children who start their vaccinations late or are more than one month behind schedule, a catch-up immunization schedule is available. This schedule provides guidance on the minimum intervals between doses and ensures that vaccinations are completed without restarting the series, regardless of the time elapsed between doses. The appropriate section of the schedule should be used based on the child’s age, and it should always be referenced alongside the general vaccination schedule and accompanying footnotes. Additionally, certain vaccines may be specifically indicated for children and adolescents under 18 years of age based on their medical conditions or specific health needs.
